region.text: northern Serbia (Rudnik, Lim lands) and the Hungarian grant of Mačva

ledger.note: 1284: Dragutin becomes King of Syrmia. After abdicating at Deževo in 1282 in favour of his brother Milutin he kept northern Serbia, and from 1284 he was 'unofficially styled King of Syrmia'; Mačva was also called Sirmia ulterior, so contemporaries called him 'King of Srem'.

region.text: Mačva, Usora and Soli (Soli read as the Tuzla salt district, Usora as Doboj: the researcher's reading)

ledger.note: Second half of 1284: Hungary grants Mačva, Usora and Soli. 'Ladislaus IV of Hungary granted Mačva, Usora and Soli to Dragutin in the second half of 1284'; 'He was the first Serbian monarch to rule Belgrade.' The page calls Usora and Soli Hungarian banates. The Dragutin page adds that Usora and Soli had been held in appanage by relatives of the Hungarian monarchs, 'most recently Dragutin's mother-in-law, Elizabeth the Cuman', and that Dragutin 'continued to rule them as a Hungarian vassal' (so they are also Hungarian vassal land for the kingdom-of-hungary dossier); the Vladislav II page calls them 'Vladislav's lands in Bosnia (Soli and Usora)'. They are drawn in the keyframes to 1324 and lost in 1325.

ledger.counterpart: Darman and Kudelin (Bulgarian boyars of Cuman origin, lords of Braničevo and Kučevo)
ledger.note: 1292: Dragutin and Milutin take Braničevo. The Darman and Kudelin page: 'In 1292, ... a joint force of Dragutin and his brother, the Serbian king Stefan Uroš II Milutin, managed to defeat Darman and Kudelin and conquered their region'; the two Bulgarian boyars of Cuman origin ruled Braničevo and Kučevo 1273-1291, repelled Hungarian troops in 1282-1284 and 1285 and 'conquered Mačva in 1290' (the page does not say from whom). The Dragutin page has Dragutin invading Braničevo 'in 1284 or 1285' and failing, then seizing it 'in 1291 or 1292, after joining forces with Milutin'; 1292 is the year both allow.

notes: Cliopatria's 'Kingdom of Syrmia' is Stefan Dragutin's realm in northern Serbia, Mačva and Belgrade; the Syrmia article it cites is a regional page that never calls Syrmia a kingdom and gives no boundaries, capital or area, so every shape verdict rests on the Dragutin page alone and the geometry is unverified (no infobox area exists to compare with Cliopatria's 24,036 km2). The Dragutin page says he was 'unofficially styled King of Syrmia' from 1284. Not on either page: how Syrmia passed in 1319 to Milutin or to Charles Robert (a common account, not opened), the end of the kingdom in 1325/1326, Debrc's coordinates (a gazetteer gap: Debrc on the Sava), Rudnik and Usora/Soli as places (the gazetteer lacks Rudnik; Usora and Soli are drawn by Tuzla and Doboj, a researcher's reading). Hungarian suzerainty: Syrmia 'was a vassal of Hungary' at first but 'later ruled independently' (Syrmia page, no dates): the kingdom-of-hungary dossier (eu-15) should carry the vassal_start (1284) and vassal_end events; the page does not date them. Counterpart strings 'Braničevo lords (page silent)' are not states. Gazetteer names needed: Rudnik, Debrc (places). Repairs of 2026-10-25 (review eu-18-d): Usora and Soli (Dragutin's Hungarian-vassal fiefs of 1284) are now part of the shape in the keyframes to 1324 (the Vladislav II page calls them 'Vladislav's lands in Bosnia (Soli and Usora)') and are lost to Stephen II of Bosnia in 1325; Rudnik is out of the shape in 1301-1311 (new keyframe _1301); the keyframes _1285, _1294 and _1314 are adjust. The 1325 date for Usora and Soli is the end of Vladislav's reign, the page gives no year. Braničevo's previous holders are Darman and Kudelin, two Bulgarian boyars of Cuman origin (ruled Braničevo and Kučevo 1273-1291, took Mačva in 1290, defeated in 1292): the date of the gain is now 1292. Start: the Syrmia page says 'Between 1282 and 1316, Syrmia was ruled by Stefan Dragutin' (tagged unreliable) and the Dragutin page has him ruling 'a separate kingdom which included northern Serbia' from the Deževo council of 1282 (infobox tenure 1282-1316), but 'unofficially styled King of Syrmia' only from 1284; the dossier starts in 1284 with Cliopatria. Still not on the pages opened: what happened to the land after Dragutin's death in 1316 beyond Milutin's undated defeat of Vladislav (before 1321), and Charles Robert's campaign of 1319; whether Dragutin lost Mačva to Darman and Kudelin in 1290-1292.
